title: Gases, pressure and the air receiver

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the pressure line running back to zero pressure at absolute zero, and pV ÷ T holding steady only in absolute units, when you drag the heat with the piston locked.
interactive.title: The sealed cylinder
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. The main picture is a sealed cylinder of gas under a piston, with a heater beneath it and one gauge with two readings. Gauge pressure is how far above the atmosphere the gas is. Absolute pressure is gauge plus the atmosphere, taken as 1 bar, so it counts from no push at all. A slider drags the piston, setting the volume from 1 to 6 L, opening at 3 L. Another sets the heater's temperature, from 0 to 150 °C, opening at 27 °C, which is 300 K. The gas starts at 2 bar absolute, 1 bar gauge. The piston has three settings: dragged, locked, or floating under a steady load. Locked holds the volume. Floating holds the pressure, so warming pushes the piston up. The heat has a lock too, which holds the temperature. A tag beside the cylinder always names what is held. Two charts follow the gas as a dot. The first plots absolute pressure, 0 to 10 bar, against volume, 0 to 6 L. With the heat locked the dot runs along a curve where pressure × volume stays the same, so half the volume gives twice the pressure. The second plots absolute pressure against temperature in °C, from −300 to 200 °C. With the piston locked the dot runs along a straight line. An Extend button draws that line on, dashed, down to zero pressure at −273 °C, absolute zero. That is where kelvin are counted from: K = °C + 273. A box shows pV ÷ T, with a three-way choice of units. In absolute pressure and kelvin it reads 0.020 bar·L/K at the start, 2 × 3 ÷ 300, and stays there whatever you drag. In gauge pressure and kelvin it starts at 1 × 3 ÷ 300 = 0.010, and pushing the piston to 1.5 L sends it to 0.015, in red. In absolute pressure and °C it starts at 2 × 3 ÷ 27, about 0.222. Warming to 127 °C with the piston locked takes the gas to about 2.67 bar absolute and sends the box to about 0.063, in red. The three readouts wrap onto two rows on a phone. A receiver skin swaps the cylinder for a 500 L air receiver and its compressor. The compressor cuts in at 6 bar gauge and cuts out at 8 bar gauge, 7 and 9 bar absolute, and that band is shaded on the gauge. Let out at 1 bar, the receiver's air at 9 bar absolute would fill 500 × 9 = 4,500 L, and at 7 bar it fills 3,500 L. So the band gives 1,000 L, shown in a readout. At an example draw of 250 L a minute, the compressor stays off for 1,000 ÷ 250 = 4 minutes. A switch doubles the receiver to 1,000 L. Its band holds 2,000 L and lasts 8 minutes, so the motor starts half as often. Screen by screen. 1 is a warm-up sum. 2 L of gas at 3 bar absolute is pushed into 1 L at the same temperature. What is its pressure? 6 bar, 1.5 bar or 4 bar absolute. A right answer says Still there. 2 shows the gauge's two readings and Boyle's law on the cylinder: with the heat locked, 3 L at 2 bar absolute pushed to 1.5 L reads 4 bar absolute, 3 bar gauge. 3 asks what a gauge reading 1 bar shows after the volume is halved at the same temperature: 3 bar, 2 bar or 4 bar. 4 shows the piston locked and the heat dragged. The pressure line is straight, and Extend runs it to zero at −273 °C. 20 °C to 40 °C is 293 K to 313 K, about 7% more. 5 asks about a locked cylinder at 2 bar absolute and 20 °C, warmed to 40 °C: about 2.1 bar, 4 bar or 2 bar absolute. 6 shows the piston floating under a steady load. Warming from 27 °C to 127 °C, 300 K to 400 K, leaves the pressure at 2 bar absolute and grows 3 L to 4 L. 7 asks what heating with the piston floating does: the pressure stays the same and the volume grows by a third, the pressure rises by a third and the volume stays the same, or both rise. 8 shows the pV ÷ T box steady in absolute units and drifting in red in gauge or °C. 9 asks about gas at 1 bar absolute, 6 L and 27 °C, pushed to 2 L and heated to 127 °C: 4 bar, 3 bar or about 14 bar absolute. 10 shows the receiver skin, the band, and the bigger receiver lasting twice as long. 11, 12 and 13 mix it all. 11: the 500 L receiver runs between 6 and 8 bar gauge. How much air at atmospheric pressure does it give from cut-out to cut-in? 1,000 L, 4,500 L or 500 L. 12: a receiver at 7 bar gauge and 20 °C warms to 50 °C. What does its gauge read? About 7.8 bar, 17.5 bar or about 8.8 bar. 13: a receiver falls from 8 to 6 bar gauge at a steady temperature. What share of its air has gone? About 22%, 25% or about 78%. A wrong pick is drawn on the charts or the box where it can be, so you see where it fails.
interactive.ignores: The gas is an ideal gas. Real gases stray from the straight line at very high pressures and near the point where they turn to liquid, so no real gas reaches zero pressure at absolute zero. The dashed line is the straight line carried on, not a measurement. The atmosphere is taken as 1 bar, though a real one is about 1.01 bar and changes with the weather and with height. A quick squeeze warms a gas, and a quick expansion against the piston cools it. Here the heater holds whatever temperature is locked, as if each move were made slowly. The piston has no friction and the cylinder never leaks. A real receiver also collects water from the air, which is drained off.

explain.text:
A trapped gas pushes on every wall around it. Squeeze it or warm it, and that push changes by a simple rule of proportion. The catch is where you count from. The rule only works when pressure and temperature are counted from true zero. One way to picture it: the push is the gas's molecules striking the walls. Halve the space and each one strikes twice as often. Warm them and they strike harder and more often.

A pressure gauge open to the air reads zero. Yet the air is pushing on it at about 1 bar. So a gauge reads how far you are above the atmosphere. That is [[gauge pressure]]. Add the atmosphere and you get [[absolute pressure]], counted from no push at all.[^3] You met Boyle's law in Proportional reasoning. Hold a gas's temperature and halve its volume, and its pressure doubles.[^2] It is the absolute pressure that doubles. A gauge reading 1 bar means the gas pushes with 2 bar in all. The gauge just leaves out the atmosphere's share. Halve the volume and the gas pushes with 4 bar absolute. So the gauge now reads 3 bar, not 2.

Temperature has the same trap. Lock the piston so the volume cannot change, then warm the gas. Its pressure climbs in a straight line. Carry that line on to colder and colder gas, and it reaches zero pressure at about −273 °C. That is absolute zero, where the kelvin scale starts. So with the volume held, the pressure is in proportion to the kelvin temperature, not the Celsius one.[^1] Warm a locked cylinder from 20 °C to 40 °C. The Celsius figure doubles, but 293 K to 313 K is only about 7% more. So the pressure rises about 7%.

What happens also depends on what is held. Let the piston float under a steady load instead, and warm the gas from 300 K to 400 K. Now the pressure stays the same, and 3 L grows to 4 L, in step with the kelvin temperature. Pressure goes up with kelvin and down with volume. So when all three change, pV ÷ T stays the same, in absolute units: p₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂V₂ ÷ T₂. Take a receiver at 7 bar gauge and 20 °C that warms to 50 °C. Its volume is held. It goes from 8 bar absolute to 8 × 323 ÷ 293, about 8.8 bar absolute, so its gauge reads about 7.8 bar. Done in gauge and Celsius, the same sum says 17.5 bar. That would more than double the pressure for 30 °C of warming, which is nonsense.

An [[air receiver]] stores air the compressor has already made. The compressor cuts in at a low pressure and out at a high one. Between starts, only the air in that band gets used. Say a 500 L receiver runs between 6 and 8 bar gauge, 7 and 9 bar absolute. By Boyle's law, its air at 9 bar would fill 4,500 L at 1 bar, and at 7 bar it fills 3,500 L. So the band gives 1,000 L. Notice that the band's width is the same 2 bar in gauge or absolute. A difference does not care where you count from. A ratio does. Double the receiver and the band holds twice the air, so the motor starts less often.[^4] Each start draws the motor's starting current, which you know from Motors. This is a simplified model, an ideal gas. Real gases stray from it at very high pressures and near turning to liquid.

**A gas's pressure, volume and temperature are in proportion only when counted from true zero, so add the atmosphere to a gauge reading and 273 to a Celsius one before any gas sum.**

analogy.text: Picture a voltmeter that takes 100 V off every reading. A 440 V supply shows 340. A 10 V drop between two points still reads 10 V, because the offset cancels in a difference. But ask it whether one voltage is twice another, and it gets it wrong. A gauge is that meter for pressure, with the atmosphere as its offset. Celsius is that meter for temperature, with 273 as its offset.
analogy.breaks: Voltage has no true zero. Every voltage is a difference between two points, so nothing is lost by choosing your reference. Pressure and temperature do have a true zero, with nothing below it, and the gas laws are written from there. And the atmosphere is not a fixed offset. It changes with the weather and with height.

practice.text:
A receiver stores a lot of energy. Before working on one or its pipework, isolate the compressor, vent the pressure and check the gauge reads zero.

- Write down what is held: the volume, the temperature or the pressure.
- Turn every gauge pressure into absolute: add the atmosphere, about 1 bar.
- Turn every Celsius temperature into kelvin: add 273.
- Use p₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂V₂ ÷ T₂, and cancel whatever is held.
- Take the atmosphere off again if a gauge will show the answer.

**Rules of thumb:** A difference comes out the same in gauge or absolute, and in °C or kelvin. A ratio needs absolute pressure and kelvin. Near room temperature, about 300 K, each 3 °C of warming raises a sealed vessel's absolute pressure by about 1%.

**Worked example:** A receiver reads 7 bar gauge at 20 °C, and the space warms to 50 °C. In absolute units that is 8 bar and 293 K, going to 323 K. The volume is held, so the pressure goes to 8 × 323 ÷ 293, about 8.8 bar absolute. The gauge reads about 7.8 bar.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting a gauge reading into a ratio. Halving the volume at 1 bar gauge gives 3 bar gauge, not 2.
- Putting Celsius into a ratio. 20 °C to 40 °C raises the pressure about 7%, not twice.
- Thinking warming always raises the pressure. It does when the volume is held. With a floating piston the volume grows instead.
- Counting all the air in a receiver as usable between starts. Only the band between cut-in and cut-out is.
